evidence: The Ramones played the Roundhouse in London on 4 July 1976 and Dingwalls on 5 July 1976 (Wikipedia's article on the band). The popular story puts members of the Sex Pistols and the Clash at the Roundhouse; both bands were in fact playing the Black Swan in Sheffield that night, the Clash's first show, supporting the Pistols (udiscovermusic's account of the Roundhouse show, and Wikipedia's list of Ramones concerts). Members of both bands, and of the Damned, are placed at the Dingwalls show the next night. Generation X's Tony James is cited in Wikipedia's article on 'Ramones' describing English bands speeding up overnight. Held at consensus because the influence is told through participants' later accounts, and the most repeated version gets the night wrong.

trackPair.whatToListenFor: 'Blitzkrieg Bop' is fast, even and relentless, every chord hit the same way, no guitar solo. 'New Rose', released in October 1976 as the first British punk single, runs at a similar sprint with a drum roll to start and barely a pause after. Listen to the tempo more than anything else. The claim on this edge is about speed: British bands already existed, and the Ramones showed them how fast and short a song could go.

explanation: The Ramones played two shows in London on 4 and 5 July 1976. Members of the Sex Pistols, the Clash and the Damned saw them, and many British punk musicians later said their own bands started playing faster after that. The influence is well attested, but the legend's details are not. The popular story says the Pistols and the Clash were at the first show, at the Roundhouse, but they were playing at the Black Swan in Sheffield that night. They saw the second one, at Dingwalls. The corrected version is also more interesting: British punk bands were already formed and playing, and what crossed the Atlantic was a speed and a song length, not the idea of punk itself.
